content: The diagnostic test on (214) is a valuable tool for determining the prevalence of Onchocerca volvulus microfilariae. The identification of heavy Loa loa infections is particularly important because high parasite loads have been associated with rare but severe adverse events (SAEs) in individuals treated with ivermectin (IVM) for onchocerciasis or lymphatic filariasis (LF). Detection of Loa loa microfilariae in the blood is possible during the daytime using methods such as thick blood smears or haemofiltration. For Onchocerca volvulus infections, adult filarial worms can be identified through nodule palpation, while ultrasound examination of lymph nodes can detect worm nests in cases of lymphatic filariasis. These methods for detecting adult worms have specific but limited applications. Antibody tests play a critical role in diagnosing filarial infections, especially in the context of Onchocerca volvulus elimination programs. By using either a single recombinant protein or a pool of recombinant proteins specific to O. volvulus, it is possible to screen subgroups within a population, such as children, for parasite-specific antibodies. This approach can confirm the interruption of transmission by demonstrating the absence of antibody responses. Similarly, mapping the prevalence of Loa loa in areas where ivermectin-induced SAEs are a concern has been achieved using antibody responses to recombinant proteins. For lymphatic filariasis, serological responses to Brugia malayi adult worm antigens are widely used in clinical diagnostics. However, when measuring antibody responses to whole parasite antigens, significant cross-reactivity with other nematode infections limits the test's specificity. Additionally, sero-reversion may be delayed. In the absence of a circulating antigen test for brugian filariasis, a dipstick antibody test has been developed to diagnose B. malayi infections, based on the antibody response to a recombinant B. malayi protein (BmR1). A major advancement in diagnosing bancroftian filariasis is the development of antigen-capture assays that detect circulating filarial antigens (CFA) of Wuchereria bancrofti. These assays allow for case-based diagnosis without requiring nocturnal blood collection, assessment of cure through clearance of antigenemia, epidemiological mapping of endemicity, and utility as a tool for elimination programs. However, equivalent tests have not been successfully developed for brugian filariasis, loiasis, or onchocerciasis. Molecular diagnostic techniques, particularly PCR-based tests, have become essential in diagnosing filariasis. PCR testing of skin scrapings for O. volvulus and blood samples for brugian and bancroftian filariasis has proven effective. Molecular xenomonitoring, which involves PCR testing of blackfly or mosquito vectors, is invaluable for epidemiological mapping of onchocerciasis and filariasis, including in elimination programs. However, as infection intensity decreases, the required sample size of insect vectors for analysis increases significantly. Despite this, elimination programs have established constant thresholds for vector analysis. Assessing infection intensity remains challenging. While there is a semi-quantitative relationship between microfilarial load (measured via blood filtration or skin snip) and adult worm burden, tools for accurately quantifying infection intensity are limited. Palpation of onchocercal nodules (onchocercomata) is only reliable in highly endemic areas and is relatively insensitive in regions of low endemicity, as up to half of Onchocerca nodules may be located in deep tissues rather than subcutaneously. Evaluating responses to antifilarial chemotherapy, including detecting anthelmintic resistance, is also problematic. Diagnostics for establishing cure are generally lacking, and the available drugs used in mass drug administration (MDA) programs are not typically macrofilaricidal, with the exception of prolonged doxycycline courses targeting Wolbachia endobacteria. For example, ivermectin does not kill adult O. volvulus worms at standard doses and intervals used in control programs. Instead, individual responses to ivermectin treatment have been studied by monitoring the reappearance rates of microfilariae in the skin after drug administration. Faster-than-expected reappearance rates may indicate suboptimal responses. Ivermectin temporarily sterilizes adult female worms, and after multiple rounds of treatment (more than 4–6 rounds), the uterus of adult female worms should be free of motile microfilariae three months post-treatment. Embryograms of worms excised from nodules approximately three months after ivermectin treatment can serve as an adjunct measure of treatment response. The disappearance of parasite antigens can also act as a surrogate marker for cure. In the context of disease mapping and surveillance, traditional parasitological methods are often too invasive and insensitive, particularly when infection prevalence falls to very low levels. Novel techniques have been developed to address these limitations. For onchocerciasis, rapid epidemiological mapping (REMO) initially relied on proximity to blackfly breeding sites and community nodule prevalence. More recently, this has been supplemented by PCR screening of pooled flies and the DEC patch test. For bancroftian filariasis, CFA assays in the form of immunochromatographic card tests (ICT) have been successfully incorporated into mapping programs. The occurrence of SAEs following ivermectin distribution in areas with high Loa loa prevalence has necessitated the development of model-based geostatistical methods to map the risk of L. loa infection exceeding a predetermined prevalence threshold (20%) in co-endemic areas. Elimination programs for onchocerciasis in the Americas and LF globally have highlighted specific deficiencies in diagnostics for filariasis in elimination settings. These include challenges in surveillance when infection prevalence drops to extremely low levels. Traditional parasitological methods are too insensitive, even with active case detection. Xenodiagnosis by PCR has been deployed in this context, but its sensitivity may be insufficient at very low transmission levels. Measuring antibody responses to specific recombinant parasite proteins has shown some utility, but these sero-epidemiological methods depend on the specificity of antibodies for single or multiple parasite target antigens. In African settings, where loiasis, bancroftian filariasis, and onchocerciasis may coexist, this problem is more pronounced than in the Americas. While encouraging, this approach poses significant logistical and financial challenges, and proof of success will only come after annual treatments cease and ongoing surveillance confirms no new infections. Mathematical modeling of filarial infections has also advanced, with deterministic and stochastic models developed for onchocerciasis and LF. These models investigate transmission dynamics, including breakpoints, and some explore parasite genetic structure and drug susceptibility to study the spread of anthelmintic resistance. However, the lack of molecular genetic markers for drug resistance and limited knowledge of population genetics hinder further progress. Research into molecular markers that can detect heritable changes in drug efficacy is crucial for mitigating the effects of resistance on control programs.
